title: 6.0001 Introduction to Computer Science and Programming in Python
description: 6.0001 Introduction to Computer Science and Programming in Python is intended for students with little or no programming experience. It aims to provide students with an understanding of the role computation can play in solving problems and to help students, regardless of their major, feel justifiably confident of their ability to write small programs that allow them to accomplish useful goals. The class will use the Python 3.5 programming language.
requiredMaterials: John Guttag. Introduction to Computation and Programming Using Python: With Application to Understanding Data, Second Edition. MIT Press, 2016. ISBN: 9780262529624. The textbook is available in hard copy or as an e-book.

policies.name: Lecture attendance
policies.text: Students are expected to attend lectures regularly because a significant portion of the course material is presented only in lecture.

policies.name: Recitation attendance
policies.text: Recitation attendance is encouraged but not required. New material may sometimes be covered in recitation.

policies.name: Problem sets and quizzes
policies.text: The course has six problem sets involving Python programming and two quizzes. Quizzes are closed-book, with one page of notes allowed for the first quiz and two pages for the second. Notes pages must be letter-sized and double-sided, and may be handwritten or typed.

policies.name: Problem-set grading
policies.text: Problem sets are graded out of 10 points. Submissions that do not run receive at most 20% of the points. Students should contact their Teaching Assistant if they have trouble understanding a problem-set grade.

policies.name: Extensions
policies.text: No extensions are granted. Late days and the option to roll at most two problem-set grades into the final quiz score are offered instead.

policies.name: Late-day allowance and accrual
policies.text: Students begin the term with two late days for problem sets. Starting with Problem Set 1, submitting an assignment early earns one late day per day before its deadline. Students may hold at most three late days at any time.

policies.name: Late-day use and tracking
policies.text: Late days must be used in whole days; half days are not allowed. Staff track the balance and include the remaining late days in each problem set’s feedback. Additional late work beyond the available late days is not accepted.

policies.name: Dropping problem sets
policies.text: Before the final quiz, an announcement will allow students to choose at most two problem sets to drop. The percentages assigned to those problem sets are rolled into the final quiz score. Late days and dropped problem sets are strongly advised as emergency backups.

policies.name: Checking submissions
policies.text: After submitting a problem set, students are advised to double-check that it uploaded correctly.

evidence.sourceExcerpt: At the beginning of the term, students are given two late days that they can use on problem sets. Starting with Problem Set 1, additional late days can be accumulated for each assignment, one late day for each day the assignment is turned in ahead of the deadline. Up to three late days may be accumulated in this fashion in this course, i.e you can only have a maximum of 3 late days at any point in time.

Late days are discrete (a student cannot use half a late day). The staff will keep track of late days and feedback for each problem set will include the number of late days the student has remaining. Any additional late work beyond these late days will not be accepted.

Before the final quiz, we will send out an announcement in which you can choose at most 2 problem sets that you can drop. If dropped, the percent that the problem sets are worth will be rolled into the final quiz score. We strongly urge you to see the late days and dropping the problem sets as backup in case of an emergency.

This is a half-semester course.
6.0001 Introduction to Computer Science and Programming in Python is intended for students with little or no programming experience.
Provide an understanding of the role computation can play in solving problems.

Help students, including those who do not plan to major in Computer Science and Electrical Engineering, feel confident of their ability to write small programs that allow them to accomplish useful goals.
Position students so that they can compete for research projects and excel in subjects with programming components.
Lectures: 2 sessions / week, 1 hour / session
Recitations: 1 sessions / week, 1 hour / session
